note: Each clip is the file the visitor sees (public/cyt), uploaded unchanged and shown at its own frame rate (all six are under 300 frames, so none is thinned). The prompt is the quiz's question, after one line giving the frame rate and, where the page itself states one, a scale cue: the two Apollo clips got "For scale, the astronaut is about 1.88 m tall.", the Aachen pendulum got "For scale, the string is about 50 cm long.", and the other three clips (both Foucault cuts and the gym ball) got no cue. The answer is held to a closed schema: verdict "real time", "slowed" or "sped up", a factor and the reasoning. Each clip was asked 5 times in separate calls, at low reasoning effort; the verdict is the majority. An earlier attempt at medium effort stopped on its second call, when an answer ran past 6000 output tokens; its spend, about $0.10 (estimated from the first call's price), is counted in usd.

A real gravity-driven pendulum with that amplitude would have a period of several seconds, but in the clip a full near-to-near oscillation takes only ~1.2 s with fast mid-swing transit and smooth harmonic turnarounds. The motion is too fast for gravity, indicating the clip is played faster than real life by about 3x.

That matches a normal gravity-driven pendulum of a few tens of cm covering 2-3m with natural speed up in the middle and dwell at the ends. No floaty slow-motion hang, no motion-blur / strobing or unnaturally fast transit that would imply high-speed or time-lapse.

Here the same distance is covered in ~1s with a floaty, smooth, stop-and-reverse without motion blur, characteristic of high-fps slow-motion played back at 25fps.

The object executes a gravity-driven pendulum-like oscillation of ~1-2m amplitude. The observed period of ~3-4s and the floaty, low-acceleration motion at the turn-around points is too slow for a ~1m physical pendulum in real time (~1.5-2s period), and the motion blur indicates faster real motion. Feet leave the ground for ~1.3-1.5s (~40 frames at 29.97 fps) for a height of ~0.3-0.4m judged against body scale, and kicked dust falls ballistically straight down. Time aloft t = 2*sqrt(2h/g). For h~0.4m, lunar g=1.62 m/s2 gives t~1.4s as observed. Earth g=9.8 would give t~0.57s, requiring ~2.5x slow-motion to match. Arm swing, knee bend and dust fall show no slow-motion float, consistent with real-time lunar gravity.

Astronaut ~1.88m tall makes a small crouch-hop of ~0.2-0.4m. In the clip the feet are off the ground for ~1.0-1.4s of the 5.2s / 156 frame @29.97fps clip. For ballistic flight t = 2*v0/g, h = v0^2/2g, so g ~ 8h/t^2 ~1-2 m/s2, i.e. lunar gravity. On Earth at real speed this hang time would require h >1m vertical jump in a bulky suit, impossible, and arm/crouch motions are normal speed, not slow-motion. Kicked dust falls ballistically and settles quickly with no air-suspension, consistent with vacuum at real speed, not slowed Earth footage.

Astronaut ~1.88 m tall jumps/hops a few tens of cm off the surface. He stays airborne ~1-1.5 s total with a slow rise and slow fall, and kicked-up dust falls ballistically straight down with no air suspension. Drop time t=sqrt(2h/g): for h~0.3-0.4 m, lunar g~1.62 m/s2 gives ~0.6-0.7 s to fall, ~1.2-1.4 s up+down, matching what is seen in ~156 frames at 29.97 fps (~5.2 s clip). Earth g=9.8 would give only ~0.25 s to fall, ~0.5 s total - far shorter. Arm swings and body motions are quick and natural, not sluggish as 2-2.5x slow-motion Earth footage made to mimic 1/6-g would be. Motion is consistent with real-time in lunar gravity.

Astronaut ~1.88m tall jumps ~0.3-0.45m off surface. He is airborne ~1.2-1.4s per jump. For h~0.4m, lunar free-fall time up+down = 2*sqrt(2h/g) with g=1.62 m/s2 is ~1.4s. Earth time for same h with g=9.81 would be ~0.57s, impossible hang. Arm swings and knee bends are at normal human speed, not slow-motion. Kicked-up soil falls ballistically straight down with no air billow, as in vacuum. No ~2.5x slow-down needed to fake lunar g is present; motion matches lunar g at real time.

Astronaut ~1.88m tall rises ~0.3-0.4m off surface and stays aloft ~1.1-1.4s of the 156 frame / 29.97fps (~5.2s) clip. For ballistic flight h = g*(t/2)^2/2, this gives g ~1.4-1.8 m/s2, matching lunar 1.62 m/s2. On Earth same effort would be aloft only ~0.5s. Arm swing shows normal-speed motion blur at 30fps, and kicked dust falls ballistically straight down with no air lofting. A 2-2.5x slow-down used to fake 1/6-g on Earth would make limb speeds sluggish and is not seen, and sped-up would shorten hang time below lunar value.
